Which of these is an official language of Ahmadiyya?
Ahmadiyya: Urdu. Adherents of the Ahmadiyya—a term adopted expressly in reference to Muhammad's alternative name Ahmad—are known as Ahmadi Muslims or simply Ahmadis.
Which of these was an official language of Goryeo?
Goryeo: Korean. Throughout its existence, Goryeo, alongside Unified Silla, was known to be the Golden Age of Buddhism in Korea.

Sasanian Empire: Middle Persian. It also helped shape European and Asian medieval art.
Which country used the Reichsmark as its official currency?
The Reichsmark is the official currency of Nazi Germany. After Hitler was appointed Chancellor of Germany in 1933, the Nazi Party began to eliminate political opposition and consolidate power.
Which Peruvian served two non-consecutive terms as president — first elected in 1985 in a landslide — as the only member of the APRA party ever to reach that office?
Alan García (Latin American; 23 May 1949 - 17 April 2019) was a Peruvian politician who served as President of Peru for two non-consecutive terms, from 1985 to 1990 and from 2006 to 2011.

Emerging from the region's Canaanite culture during the Iron Age, two neighboring biblical kingdoms in the Southern Levant are first mentioned by name on an Egyptian inscription from around 1208 BCE — which two kingdoms?
Ancient Israel and Judah were two Israelite kingdoms that existed in the Southern Levant during the Iron Age.

Grand Duchess Tatiana Nikolaevna of Russia
Asenath (Koine) is a minor figure in the Book of Genesis.
A former SAS trooper turned wilderness-TV host, in 2009 he became the Scout Association's youngest-ever Chief Scout at age 35 — who is this British adventurer?
Bear Grylls (born 7 June 1974) is a British adventurer, television presenter and former SAS trooper.

Before founding the party Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam and becoming chief minister of Tamil Nadu in 2026, this man was one of India's highest-paid Tamil cinema stars — making his leading debut in a 1992 film directed by his own father. Who is he?
C. Joseph Vijay (born 22 June 1974) is an Indian politician and former actor who is currently serving as the ninth chief minister of Tamil Nadu since May 2026.
Nicknamed the 'Father-in-law of Europe' for marrying his children into so many royal houses, which Danish king reigned from 1863 to 1906?
Christian IX (8 April 1818 - 29 January 1906) was King of Denmark from 15 November 1863 until his death in 1906.
This American anthropologist and anarchist gave the Occupy movement a leading voice and wrote provocative books like Debt: The First 5,000 Years and Bullshit Jobs — who was he?
David Graeber (February 12, 1961 - September 2, 2020) was an American anthropologist and anarchist social and political activist.
Often called the greatest jurist of the Elizabethan and Jacobean eras, this English barrister rose from the Inner Temple to Speaker of the House of Commons and Attorney General. Who was he?
Edward Coke (CUUK, formerly; 1 February 1552 - 3 September 1634) was an English barrister, judge, and politician.
Ascending to the Iraqi throne at age three after his father's death, this monarch was killed in the 1958 coup that ended the Hashemite monarchy — who is he?
Faisal II (2 May 1935 - 14 July 1958) was the last King of Iraq.

An Egyptian military revolutionary seized power in 1954, introduced sweeping land reforms, and became a hero across the Arab world by nationalizing a crucial waterway. Who led Egypt as its second president for sixteen transformative years?
Gamal Abdel Nasser (15 January 1918 - 28 September 1970) was an Egyptian military officer and revolutionary who served as the second president of Egypt from 1954 until his death in 1970.
This art-collecting Russian general and patron helped install Catherine the Great on the throne before his infidelities cost him his influence — who is he?
Grigory Orlov (17 October 1734 - 24 April 1783) was a Russian general and patron of arts who was Prince of the Holy Roman Empire (1772) and a favourite of Empress Catherine the Great.
House speaker, secretary of state, and a three-time loser of the presidency, this Kentuckian earned the nickname 'the Great Compromiser' for defusing sectional crises — who was he?
Henry Clay (April 12, 1777 - June 29, 1852) was an American lawyer, statesman, and diplomat who represented Kentucky in both the United States House of Representatives and the United States Senate.
Son of a former prime minister, this Cambodian leader rose through the Royal Cambodian Army to deputy commander-in-chief before taking his father's job in 2023 — who is he?

Hun Manet (born 20 October 1977) is a Cambodian politician and military officer who has served as Prime Minister of Cambodia and Vice President of the ruling Cambodian People's Party (CPP) since 2023.
This mid-1740s bid to restore the exiled Stuarts to the British throne began in the Scottish Highlands and ended when its army turned back from Derby in December — which rebellion?
Jacobite rising of 1745 was an attempt to regain the British throne for the exiled House of Stuart.

This German-American newspaper editor and orator popularized 'propaganda of the deed' in the United States and was jailed several times after publishing literature on how to build and use bombs — who was he?
Johann Most (February 5, 1846 - March 17, 1906) was a German-American Social Democratic and then anarchist politician, newspaper editor, and orator.
This Indian politician has served since 2024 as both Minister of Communications and Minister of Development of the North Eastern Region — who is he?
Jyotiraditya Scindia (born 1 January 1971; Hindi) is an Indian politician who is serving as the 43rd Minister of Communications and 10th Minister of Development of North Eastern Region since 2024.

Co-recipient with the United Nations of the 2001 Nobel Peace Prize, this Ghanaian diplomat served as the organization's seventh secretary-general and later chaired an international group founded by Nelson Mandela — who was he?
Kofi Annan (8 April 1938 - 18 August 2018) was a Ghanaian diplomat and statesman who served as the seventh secretary-general of the United Nations from 1997 to 2006.
Once seen as Mao Zedong's likely successor, this Chinese politician served as head of state from 1959 until he was purged during the Cultural Revolution — who was he?
Liu Shaoqi (24 November 1898 - 12 November 1969) was a Chinese revolutionary and politician.
Orphaned of his father at three, this Roman emperor became the last of the Five Good Emperors and is remembered as much for his Stoic philosophy as his reign — who was he?
Marcus Aurelius (26 April 121 - 17 March 180) was Roman emperor from 161 to 180 and a Stoic philosopher.
Said to have lived 969 years — the longest recorded lifespan in the Bible — this patriarch was the grandfather of Noah — who is he?
Methuselah was a biblical patriarch and a figure in Judaism, Christianity, and Islam.
Possibly Arthur's own son in early Welsh tradition, this Arthurian figure was later recast as a treacherous nephew associated with the fateful Battle of Camlann. Who is he?
Mordred (or) is a major figure in the legend of King Arthur.
Born at Tsarskoye Selo and widely thought ill-prepared to rule, this monarch led his empire into World War I before abdicating in 1917 — and in 1918 his whole family was murdered. Who was he?
Nicholas II was Emperor of Russia from 1894 to 1917.
Once Britain's youngest sitting MP, this baronet drifted from the Conservatives to Labour before founding the British Union of Fascists in 1932 — who is it?
Oswald Mosley (16 November 1896 - 3 December 1980), was a British politician who rose to fame during the 1920s and 1930s when, disillusioned with mainstream politics, he turned to fascism.
This longtime CPI(M) state secretary became Kerala's 12th Chief Minister in 2016 and later served as Leader of the Opposition — who is he?
Pinarayi Vijayan (born 24 May 1945) is an Indian politician who served as the 12th Chief Minister of Kerala from 25 May 2016 to 18 May 2026.
Charged with murder after a deadly 1992 standoff with federal agents at his Idaho cabin, this self-proclaimed separatist was ultimately acquitted of most charges — who is he?
Randy Weaver (January 3, 1948 - May 11, 2022) was an American survivalist and self-proclaimed white separatist.
He was the longest-serving commandant of Auschwitz, in charge across two stretches between 1940 and 1945 — what was his name?
Rudolf Höss (also H, Hoe, or Hoess; 25 November 1901 - 16 April 1947) was a German SS officer and the commandant of the Auschwitz concentration camp.
Briefly governor of Moscow Oblast in 2012, this member of Putin's inner circle led Russia's defence ministry until 2024, when he moved to secretary of the Security Council — who is he?
Sergei Shoigu (born 21 May 1955) is a Russian politician and military officer who has served as secretary of the Security Council since 2024.
Gaining wide use in American political discourse of the 1930s and '40s, this doctrine holds that governing authority carries some legitimacy, standing opposed to anarchism — what's it called?
Statism (from French, tat 'state') is the doctrine that the political authority of the state is legitimate to some degree.
Before he became the Supreme Court's first African-American justice, this lawyer won 29 of the 32 civil rights cases he argued there, capped by 1954's Brown v. Board of Education — who is he?
Thurgood Marshall (July 2, 1908 - January 24, 1993) was an American lawyer who served as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States from 1967 until 1991.
Spanning roughly 800 to 1050 CE, this era saw Scandinavian raiders, traders, and settlers push across Europe and reach as far as North America — which age?

Viking Age (about 800-1050 CE) was the period during the Middle Ages when Norsemen known as Vikings undertook large-scale raiding, colonising, conquest, and trading throughout Europe and reached North America.
Starting in his father's grocery business at fifteen, this English industrialist built an empire on Sunlight Soap, Lux, and Lifebuoy. Who was he?
William Lever, 1st Viscount Leverhulme (19 September 1851 - 7 May 1925) was an English industrialist, philanthropist, and politician.

This Soviet partisan was executed by invading Nazi forces after committing acts of sabotage, and was posthumously declared a Hero of the Soviet Union, becoming one of its most revered heroines — who was she?
Zoya Kosmodemyanskaya (September 13, 1923 - November 29, 1941) was a Soviet partisan.
Traditionally chanted by a muezzin from a mosque's minaret before each of the five daily prayers, what is this Islamic call known as?
Adhan: Islamic call to prayer. The five prayer times are known in Arabic as fajr (فجر), dhuhr (ظهر), asr (عصر), maghrib (مغرب), and isha (عشاء).
Despite never attending Germany's War Academy, this WWI balloon observer rose to become a highly decorated Luftwaffe field marshal in World War II — who was he?
The second sultan of the Seljuk Empire, this ruler's decisive 1071 victory over the Byzantines at Manzikert opened Anatolia to Turkoman settlement — who is he?
Alp Arslan: Sultan of the Seljuk Empire from 1063 to 1072.
Arrested in the US in 2010 as part of a Russian espionage ring, this former agent-turned-media personality was later swapped back to Russia in a prisoner exchange — who is she?
Anna Chapman: Russian intelligence agent, media personality and model (born 1982)
A onetime communist who embraced privatization, this physicist-turned-leader ran Kyrgyzstan from 1990 until 2005, when the Tulip Revolution swept him from power. Who was he?

Askar Akayev: President of Kyrgyzstan from 1990 to 2005. Akayev became president of Kyrgyzstan in 1990, a year before the Fall of the Soviet Union, and he remained in his post after Kyrgyzstan became independent.
Worshipped since Egypt's Second Dynasty and known to the Greeks as Ailuros, or 'cat', this goddess embodied a gentler counterpart to the fierce lioness deity Sekhmet — who is she?

Drawing on Bolshevism and anarchism, this Indian revolutionary's largely symbolic bombing of the Central Legislative Assembly and a jail hunger strike made him a folk hero — and a martyr after his execution at age 23; who was he?
It began in 1703 as a townhouse for a duke, then George III bought it in 1761 as a private home for Queen Charlotte — today it's a monarch's official London residence. Which building?

Buckingham Palace: Official London residence of the British monarch. Buckingham Palace (UK:) is the official residence and the administrative headquarters of the monarch of the United Kingdom in London.
Derived from the Latin word for 'to assess,' this systematic count of a population's members is recommended by the UN to be conducted at least once every ten years. What is it?
Census: Compilation of information about a given population.

Growing up on the coast of Liguria, this explorer traveled as far north as the British Isles and as far south as present-day Ghana before commanding four Spanish transatlantic voyages—opening the door to European colonization of the Americas. Who was he?
Christopher Columbus: Italian navigator and explorer (1451–1506)

Sparked by Tsar Nicholas I's demand that the Ottoman Empire's Orthodox subjects be placed under his protection, this 1853–1856 conflict pitted Russia against an alliance that included Britain, France, and Sardinia-Piedmont — which war is it?
Crimean War: Tenth conflict of the Russo-Turkish wars (1853–1856)
On 30 April 1945, as the Battle of Berlin was lost, a man in the Führerbunker shot himself a day after marrying Eva Braun, who took cyanide — which grim historical event is this?
Death of Adolf Hitler: 1945 suicide of German dictator.

Fought between 1568 and 1648, this conflict between Dutch rebels and the Spanish crown is also known as the Dutch Revolt, and saw William the Silent unite Catholic and Protestant provinces under the Pacification of Ghent — what was it?
Eighty Years' War: c. 1566/1568–1648 war in Habsburg Netherlands.
Leading the Communist Party of Germany from 1925 to 1933, this revolutionary sought to overthrow the Weimar Republic and branded rival Social Democrats as 'social fascists' — who is he?
The son of a wealthy Spanish farmer, this Cuban revolutionary picked up anti-imperialist ideas studying law in Havana before ruling the island from 1959 to 2008 — who was he?
Fidel Castro: Leader of Cuba from 1959 to 2008.
Governing France from the fall of Napoleon III in 1870 until the Nazi invasion of 1940, this parliamentary system weathered the Paris Commune and the loss of Alsace-Lorraine — what was it?

French Third Republic: Government of France from 1870 to 1940. Consequently, the Third Republic, originally envisioned as a provisional government, instead became the permanent form of government of France.
Alabama's longest-serving governor, he ran for the U.S. presidency four times and in 1968 carried five states for a third party — a feat unseen since 1948. Who was this Democrat?
George Wallace: American politician and lawyer (1919–1998)
In 2018, a 15-year-old skipped class to sit alone outside Sweden's parliament — and accidentally sparked the worldwide Fridays for Future movement. Which young climate activist was it?
This 10th-century king introduced Christianity to Denmark and united Jutland and Zealand under his rule, before being ousted by his own son — who was he?

Harald Bluetooth: 10th-century King of Denmark and Norway. Harald "Bluetooth" Gormsson (Old Norse: Haraldr Blátǫnn Gormsson; Danish: Harald Blåtand Gormsen, died c. 985/86) was a king of Denmark and Norway.
Also known as the White Huns, this Central Asian people defeated the Kidarites in 450 CE before falling to a joint Turkic-Sasanian force in 560 — who were they?
Hephthalites: 5th–8th-century nomadic confederation in Central Asia.

This cadet branch of the Capetian line ruled France from 1328 to 1589, spinning off junior branches in Orléans, Anjou, Burgundy, and Alençon before its male line died out and the Bourbons took over — which royal dynasty?
House of Valois: Cadet branch of the Capetian dynasty. The Capetian House of Valois (VAL-wah, also US: va(h)l-WAH, French: [valwa]) was a cadet branch of the Capetian dynasty.
A locksmith's apprentice turned committed communist, this Hungarian politician led the 1956 uprising against the Soviet-backed government — and was executed for it two years later. Who was he?
Imre Nagy: Hungarian politician and leader of the 1956 revolution (1896–1958)
Ruling Kuwait from 1977 until his death in 2006, this emir led the country through the Gulf War against Saddam Hussein's Iraq with US backing — who is he?
Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah: Emir of Kuwait from 1977 to 2006. The 13th ruler in his family's dynasty, Jaber's reign oversaw the transition of a relatively traditional society into a modernized state.
Leader of La France Insoumise, this French politician has run for president three times and announced a fourth bid for 2027 — who is he?
His eleven years in the top job make him Australia's second-longest-serving prime minister, trailing only Robert Menzies — which member of parliament for Bennelong led the country from 1996 to 2007?
John Howard: Prime Minister of Australia from 1996 to 2007. Howard was born in Sydney and studied law at the University of Sydney.

Charles I of Spain awarded this navigator a coat of arms reading "Primus circumdedisti me" — "You were the first to circumnavigate me" — after he completed the first voyage around the Earth aboard the Victoria. Who was he?
Juan Sebastián Elcano: Spanish seafarer and circumnavigator.
Symbolized by the Six Arrows, this political ideology stemmed from the sweeping secularizing reforms of Turkey's founding president — which ideology is it?
Kemalism: Founding ideology of the Republic of Türkiye.
A towering figure whose political career spanned seven decades, this Greek statesman served four terms as prime minister and two as president of the Third Hellenic Republic — who was he?
The 17th king of Sparta's Agiad dynasty, which claimed descent from Heracles, he led the allied Greek last stand at Thermopylae against the Persians; who was he?
Leonidas I: King of Sparta from c. 489 BC to 480 BC.

Crowned King of France just before his ninth birthday after his father Henry IV was assassinated, this monarch later seized power by exiling his own mother and executing her favorite, Concino Concini — who was he?
Louis XIII: King of France from 1610 to 1643.

Because British insurers wouldn't pay claims tied to a "civil war," colonial officials coined a euphemistic name for this 1948-1960 guerrilla conflict against communist independence fighters — which conflict?
Malayan Emergency: 1948–1960 British colonial war in Malaya. The communists gained support from many civilians, mainly those from the Chinese community.
Serving as Bavaria's Minister-President since 2018, this German politician has also led the region's dominant conservative party since 2019 — who is he?
A former physician, she became First Lady of Azerbaijan and, in 2017, was appointed by her husband the president to a newly created role as First Vice President — who is she?
Mehriban Aliyeva: First Vice President of Azerbaijan since 2017.
Described in the Hebrew Bible as the older sister of Moses and Aaron, this prophetess led the Israelite women out of Egypt and taught them Torah — who is she?
Miriam: Sister of Moses and Aaron. The Torah refers to her as "Miriam the Prophetess" and the Talmud names her as one of the seven major female prophets of Israel.
Nicknamed 'Netaji' by his party, this Indian politician founded the Samajwadi Party and served three terms as Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh — who is he?
Launched in 2017 by Crown Prince Mohammad bin Salman, this Saudi megaproject at the northern tip of the Red Sea was eventually scaled way back amid delays, cost overruns, and criticism — what is it?
Neom: Planned city in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.
Renowned for his cunning intelligence, this legendary king of Ithaca spent ten eventful years just trying to get home after the Trojan War — who is he?
Odysseus: Legendary Greek king of Ithaca. Odysseus also plays a key role in Homer's Iliad and other works in that same epic cycle.

Known to the Rus as the Obri and to the Göktürks as the Apar, this nomadic confederation ruled a khaganate centered on the Carpathian Basin from the late sixth to early ninth centuries — who were they?
Pannonian Avars: Alliance of various Eurasian nomads – 6th to 9th centuries.

Born in what is now Syria, this Roman emperor reigned from 244 to 249 during an unusually stable stretch of a turbulent century, after being proclaimed ruler when his predecessor died in battle — who is he?
Philip the Arab: Roman emperor from 244 to 249. Philip I (Latin: Marcus Julius Philippus; c. 204 – September 249), commonly known as Philip the Arab, was Roman emperor from 244 to 249.
A member of India's storied Nehru dynasty, this Indian National Congress politician has represented Wayanad in Kerala in the Lok Sabha since November 2024 — who is she?

Rooted in a Greek word meaning 'to snatch away' from First Thessalonians, this end-times evangelical belief holds that living and dead Christians alike will rise to meet Christ in the clouds — what is it called?
This three-time Conservative prime minister, who doubled as Foreign Secretary for most of his tenure, championed a foreign policy he called 'splendid isolation' — who was he?
Robert Cecil, Viscount Cecil of Chelwood
Robert Gascoyne-Cecil, 3rd Marquess of Salisbury: British prime minister (1885-86; 1886-92; 1895-1902)
An Iraqi politician who served as the fifth president from 1979 until his overthrow in 2003 during the US-led invasion, previously a vice president and prime minister—who was he?
Saddam Hussein: President of Iraq from 1979 to 2003. The policies and ideologies he championed are collectively known as Saddamism, a right-wing variant of Ba'athism.
This Roman general's victory over Hannibal at the Battle of Zama in 202 BC earned him an honorific epithet referencing the continent he conquered — who was he?
Scipio Africanus: Roman general and politician (236/235 – c. 183 BC)
Daughter of Bangladesh's first president, she became the country's longest-serving prime minister and one of the world's longest-serving female heads of government — who is she?
Sheikh Hasina: Prime Minister of Bangladesh (1996–2001; 2009–2024)
Born in Požarevac and a law graduate of Belgrade, he became the first sitting head of state ever charged with war crimes — which Serbian president, overthrown in 2000?
Slobodan Milošević: Yugoslav and Serbian politician (1941–2006)
Flourishing along the Tigris and Euphrates in southern Mesopotamia, this is considered the earliest known civilization, home to the world's oldest surviving texts from Uruk — what was it called?
Sumer: Ancient Mesopotamian civilization from 3300 to 1900 BC.
Launched as a surprise strike during the Lunar New Year — when most South Vietnamese troops were on leave — this 1968 campaign became one of the Vietnam War's largest. What was it?
Tet Offensive: 1968 Vietnam War military campaign. The Tet Offensive was both a major escalation and one of the largest military campaigns of the Vietnam War.
The military government of Japan from 1603 to 1868, established after the Battle of Sekigahara and based in Edo Castle—what is this shogunate called?
Tokugawa shogunate: 1603–1868 Japanese military government (Edo Jidai)
As third caliph of the Rashidun Caliphate, this son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad ordered the standardized compilation of the Quran still used today — who was he?
This Ukrainian-born Russian military blogger and convicted bank robber, who became a pro-war propagandist, was assassinated in a Saint Petersburg bombing in April 2023 — who was he?

Vladlen Tatarsky: Russian military blogger (1982–2023). Tatarsky was active as a propagandist for Russia and the separatist forces in Ukraine until he was assassinated in a bombing in Saint Petersburg in April 2023.

Serving four non-consecutive terms as British Prime Minister between 1868 and 1894 — more than anyone else — this Liverpool-born statesman began as a Conservative MP before becoming the face of the Liberal Party — who was he?
Serving as head of state under Lenin's new government until his death in 1919, this Bolshevik organizer of the October Revolution also chaired the party's Secretariat — who was he?
Son of Edward the Elder, this ruler is regarded by modern historians as the first King of England; he never married and was succeeded by his half-brother Edmund — who is he?
Æthelstan: King of the English from 927 to 939.

Henry Vaughan (born 1621) is the earliest of the four. Henry Vaughan (1621 – 23 April 1695) was a Welsh metaphysical poet, author and translator writing in English, and a medical physician.
Which of these four has been around longest?
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four. COBOL (Common Business-Oriented Language;) is a compiled English-like computer programming language designed for business use.
Which of these four was founded earliest?

Fortran (founded 1957) is the earliest of the four. Fortran (formerly FORTRAN) is a third-generation, compiled, imperative programming language designed for numeric computation and scientific computing.
Who among these is a physicist?
Louis Slotin is a physicist. Louis Alexander Slotin ( SLOHT-in; 1 December 1910 – 30 May 1946) was a Canadian physicist and chemist who took part in the Manhattan Project.
Pick the chemist from these four.
James Lovelock is a chemist. James Ephraim Lovelock (26 July 1919 – 26 July 2022) was an English independent scientist, environmentalist and futurist.
What is the atomic number of Unbiunium?
Unbiunium, also known as eka-actinium or element 121, is a hypothetical chemical element; it has symbol Ubu and atomic number 121.
In what year was J. Robert Oppenheimer born?
J. Robert Oppenheimer: In 1941, Oppenheimer was briefed about nuclear weapon design by Australian physicist Mark Oliphant.
In what year did Archimedes die?
Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, when he was killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed.
In what year was Iron discovered?
Iron is a chemical element; it has symbol Fe (from Latin ferrum 'iron') and atomic number 26.
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-25: Russian Aircraft Corporation MiG. Designed by the Soviet Union's Mikoyan-Gurevich bureau, it is an aircraft built primarily using stainless steel.
Which country is Sukhoi Su-57 from?
Sukhoi Su-57: Russia. The Sukhoi Su-57 (Russian: Сухой Су-57; NATO reporting name: Felon) is a twin-engine stealth multirole fighter aircraft developed by Sukhoi.
Who is credited with discovering Gaussian integral?
Gaussian integral: Leonhard Euler. The integral has a wide range of applications.
Who is credited with discovering Aspirin?
Aspirin: Raffaele Piria. Aspirin is used to treat inflammatory conditions including Kawasaki disease, pericarditis, and rheumatic fever.
Who is credited with discovering Boron?
Boron: Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac. Boron is a chemical element; it has symbol B and atomic number 5.

The active component of vinegar and the second simplest carboxylic acid, this colourless liquid with the formula CH₃COOH has been produced in large quantities since the third millennium BCE. What is this acid?
Acetic acid is an acidic, colourless liquid and organic compound with the chemical formula CH3COOH (also written as CH3CO2H, C2H4O2, or HC2H3O2).
A military pilot who became the first astronaut representing Turkey, he reached the International Space Station on 18 January 2024 aboard the Axiom Mission 3 flight — who is he?
Alper Gezeravcı (born 2 December 1979) is a military pilot and the first Turkish astronaut.
What term describes the discipline of measuring human body dimensions, applied everywhere from ergonomics and architecture to tracking historical living standards?
Anthropometry (from Ancient Greek (nthrpos) 'human' and (mtron) 'measure') refers to the measurement of the human individual.

Distinguished from celestial mechanics by asking what heavenly bodies ARE rather than where they are, this science applies physics and chemistry to the Sun, stars, galaxies, and exoplanets — which discipline?
Astrophysics is a science that applies the methods and principles of physics and chemistry in the study of astronomical objects and phenomena including the universe.
This steroid medication treats conditions ranging from rheumatoid arthritis and psoriasis to asthma, and is also given before preterm birth to help speed a baby's lung development — what drug is it?
Betamethasone is a steroid medication. It can be taken by mouth, injected into a muscle, or applied to the skin, typically in cream, lotion, or liquid forms.

Derived from Greek words for 'slow' and 'heart', this medical term describes a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute — sometimes a red flag, sometimes just a sign of a well-conditioned athlete. Name the condition?
Bradycardia (brads), meaning "slow", and (karda), meaning "heart", also called bradyarrhythmia, is a resting heart rate under 60 beats per minute (BPM).
Caused by an overgrowth of a common yeast, this fungal infection is known as thrush when it affects the mouth and can also cause a genital yeast infection — name the condition?
Candidiasis is a fungal infection due to any species of yeasts in the genus Candida or those that were formerly classified in genus Candida but are now classified in the genus Candidozyma.
Despite no clinical evidence it treats any disease, this daisy-like plant is a staple in calming herbal tea, beer brewing, and even garden ground cover — what is it?
Chamomile (American English) or camomile (British English; see spelling differences) (or) is the common name for several daisy-like plants of the family Asteraceae.
Born near Toulouse, this French inventor is remembered chiefly as an aviation pioneer — though in 1870 he was also an early enthusiast of cycling in France; who was he?
Clément Ader (French; 2 April 1841 - 3 May 1925) was a French inventor and engineer who was born near Toulouse in Muret, Haute-Garonne, and died in Toulouse.
Going by puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther depending on the region, this big cat is the most widely distributed wild land mammal in the Western Hemisphere — what is it?
Cougar (Puma concolor), also called puma, mountain lion, catamount, and panther, is a large feline native to the Americas.
Caused by either too little insulin or cells that ignore it, this condition keeps blood sugar stubbornly high and comes chiefly in a type 1 and a type 2 — what is it?
Diabetes is a group of common endocrine diseases characterized by sustained high blood sugar levels.
This social science examines the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services, analyzing everything from individual agents to entire economies. What discipline is this?
Economics is a social science that studies the production, distribution, and consumption of goods and services.
This class of mental health condition is defined by an enduring, pervasive pattern of behavior, emotion, and thought that deviates from social norms and develops early in life. What is it?
Erythritol is an organic compound, the naturally occurring achiral meso four-carbon sugar alcohol (or polyol).
Which evergreen conifer genus has needle-like leaves attached singly to the branch by a circular base, and cones that stand upright like a cedar's rather than hanging down? What is it?
Fir are evergreen coniferous trees belonging to the genus Abies in the family Pinaceae.
Native to Pacific coastal waters from Alaska to Baja California, this giant burrowing clam can grow a siphon over three feet long and live for more than a century — which creature?
Geoduck (Panopea generosa) is a species of very large saltwater clam in the family Hiatellidae.

These common coastal seabirds, most closely related to terns and skimmers, were once known by an older name still surviving in some English dialects and cognate with the German word Möwe — what birds are they?
Gull (see Taxonomy), are seabirds of the subfamily Larinae.
First identified in 1910, this organic compound is stored in mast cells and basophils and, though not made by classic endocrine glands, still acts as a local hormone — what compound is it?
Histamine is an organic nitrogenous compound found in mammals and many vegetables, fruits and food products.

For decades this University of Virginia psychiatrist ran a Division of Perceptual Studies and gathered evidence that memories — and even bodily features — might carry across lives. Which researcher into reincarnation was he?

Ian Stevenson (October 31, 1918 - February 8, 2007) was a Canadian-born American psychiatrist, the founder and director of the Division of Perceptual Studies at the University of Virginia School of Medicine.

This American scientist co-authored a landmark 1953 paper with Francis Crick proposing the double-helix structure of DNA, building on research by Rosalind Franklin, and shared a 1962 Nobel Prize for the discovery — who is he?
James Watson (April 6, 1928 - November 6, 2025) was an American molecular biologist, geneticist, and zoologist.

Sharing the 1973 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, this ethologist was among the first to decode the honey bee's waggle dance — a theory greeted with such skepticism that it took decades to be vindicated. Who was he?
Karl von Frisch (20 November 1886 - 12 June 1982) was a German-Austrian ethologist who received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine in 1973, along with Nikolaas Tinbergen and Konrad Lorenz.

This Hungarian-born physicist conceived the nuclear chain reaction in 1933, drafted the famous letter Einstein signed to launch the Manhattan Project, then later petitioned President Truman not to drop the bomb on civilians — who was he?

Leo Szilard (born Le Spitz; February 11, 1898 - May 30, 1964) was a Hungarian-born American physicist, biologist and inventor who made numerous important discoveries in nuclear physics and the biological sciences.
Reclassified in 2021 as part of the order Psocodea alongside booklice and barklice, these tiny wingless parasites cement their eggs to a single host for life — what are they called?
Louse (pl.: lice) is the common name for any member of the infraorder Phthiraptera, which contains nearly 5,000 species of wingless parasitic insects.
Google's employee No. 20 and its first woman software engineer, she later left to run a famous internet company as CEO from 2012 until Verizon bought it — who is she?
Marissa Mayer (born May 30, 1975) is an American business executive, software engineer, and investor who served as president and chief executive officer of Yahoo!
What neurological disorder causes moderate-to-severe, often one-sided headaches, frequently accompanied by nausea, light and sound sensitivity, and sometimes preceded by a sensory 'aura'?
Migraine is a neurological disorder that causes moderate-to-severe headaches. The pain usually affects one side of the head.
With somewhere between 66 and 70 species across nine subfamilies, this carnivore family stretches from tiny weasels all the way up to the wolverine. What is it?
Mustelidae (from Latin mustela, weasel) are a diverse family of carnivoran mammals, including weasels, badgers, otters, sea otters, polecats, martens, grisons and wolverines.

Considered primary if a child has never had a long dry stretch, this common childhood condition — usually a developmental delay rather than an illness — is commonly called bedwetting. What's its clinical name?
Nocturnal enuresis (NE), also informally called bedwetting, is involuntary urination while asleep after the age at which bladder control usually begins.
Derived from an ancient Roman unit called the uncia, this unit of mass equals 1/16 of a pound in its common form, though a heavier 'troy' version weighs precious metals — name the unit?
Ounce is any of several different units of mass, weight, or volume and is derived almost unchanged from the uncia, an Ancient Roman unit of measurement.

This short-acting barbiturate is used as a sedative and anticonvulsant in low doses, but in high doses causes fatal respiratory arrest, making it a drug of choice for both veterinary euthanasia and U.S. executions — what is it?
Pentobarbital (US) or pentobarbitone (British and Australian) is a short-acting barbiturate typically used as a sedative, a preanesthetic, and to control convulsions in emergencies.
Native to Eurasia and identifiable by short, blue-green needles, this member of the pine family goes by several regional common names — name the species (Latin binomial)?
Pinus sylvestris is a species of tree in the pine family Pinaceae that is native to Eurasia.
Split into the strepsirrhines — lemurs and lorisids — and the haplorhines — tarsiers, monkeys and apes — this order ranges in size down to tiny Madame Berthe's — what is it?

Primate is an order of mammals, which is further divided into the strepsirrhines, which include lemurs, galagos, and lorisids; and the haplorhines, which include tarsiers and simians (monkeys and apes).

Founding an organization promoting swadeshi economics against globalization, this Indian social activist later allied with a yoga guru to combine that economic message with the promotion of yoga and Ayurveda — who is he?
Rajiv Dixit (30 November 1967 - 30 November 2010) was an Indian social activist who founded the Azadi Bachao Andolan.

This English X-ray crystallographer's photographs were crucial to unraveling the structure of DNA, yet her contribution went largely unrecognized in her lifetime, earning her posthumous nicknames like "the wronged heroine" — who was she?
Rosalind Franklin (25 July 1920 - 16 April 1958) was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer.
With segmented bony armor, an upright posture, and a curling prehensile tail, these 46 species of tiny bony fish are cousins to the pipefishes and seadragons — what are they?
Seahorse (also written sea-horse and sea horse) is any of 46 species of small marine bony fish in the genus Hippocampus.
Once placed alone in the genus Uncia before phylogenetics moved it into Panthera, this high-altitude cat ranges across the Tibetan Plateau and Himalayas — what is it?
Snow leopard (Panthera uncia) is a species of large cat in the genus Panthera of the family Felidae.
Lacking the powder down that herons and ibises use to clean off fish slime, these bill-clattering wading birds come in 20 living species across six genera — which birds?
Stork are large, long-legged, long-necked wading birds with long, stout bills.

Equal to one weber per square metre, this SI unit of magnetic flux density was adopted in 1960 and named for a Serbian-American electrical engineer, on the proposal of a Slovenian engineer — name this unit?
Tesla (unit) (symbol: T) is the unit of magnetic flux density (B) (also called magnetic B-field) in the International System of Units (SI).
Roughly eight times more potent than an older analogue, this bleeding-control medication is also prescribed for hereditary angioedema — what is it?
Tranexamic acid is a medication used to treat or prevent excessive blood loss from major trauma, postpartum bleeding, surgery, tooth removal, nosebleeds, and heavy menstruation.
This British-American structural biologist shared the 2009 Nobel in Chemistry for revealing the ribosome's structure and later led the Royal Society as president — who is he?
Venki Ramakrishnan (born 1952) is a British-American structural biologist.
Marketed under names like Rompun, this veterinary sedative and alpha-2 adrenergic agonist is often combined with ketamine for animal anesthesia and used as an emetic in cats — what is it?

Xylazine is a structural analog of clonidine and an 2-adrenergic receptor agonist, sold under many trade names worldwide, most notably the Bayer brand name Rompun, as well as Anased, Sedazine and Chanazine.
Known by the common name yarrow, this pungent, fernleaved plant in the daisy family is used in traditional medicine and as livestock feed — what is its scientific name?
Achillea millefolium: Species of plant. Achillea millefolium, commonly known as yarrow or common yarrow, is a flowering plant in the family Asteraceae.
A former IMF economist, this politician has served as President of Ivory Coast since 2010 after earlier stints as the country's prime minister in the early 1990s — who is he?
Alassane Ouattara: President of Ivory Coast since 2010. Ouattara became the president of the Rally of the Republicans (RDR), an Ivorian political party, in 1999.
Also known as shadbush, serviceberry, or juneberry, this rose-family shrub's berries inspired the name of a Canadian city — which genus?
First described by a German entomologist in 1818 and known as the 'marsh mosquito,' this genus is the only one that transmits malaria to humans — which genus is it?
Anopheles: Genus of mosquito. The genus Anopheles diverged from other mosquitoes approximately 100 million years ago (mya), and, like other mosquitoes, the eggs, larvae, and pupae are aquatic.
The third most abundant gas in Earth's atmosphere at nearly 1%, this noble gas takes its name from an Ancient Greek word meaning 'lazy' or 'inactive' — what element is it?
Argon: Chemical element with atomic number 18 (Ar)
Native to tropical Southeast Asia, this small tree bears bell-shaped rose-to-purple flowers and a ridged fruit that forms star-shaped slices when cut crosswise — which species?
Averrhoa carambola: Species of tree. It is a small tree or shrub that grows 5 to 12 m (16 to 39 ft) tall, with rose to red-purple flowers.
Sometimes called the common, lawn, or English variety, this European plant is considered the archetypal member of the daisy family — what's its scientific name?

Bellis perennis: Species of plant in the daisy family. Bellis perennis ( BEL-iss pə-REN-iss), the daisy, is a European species of the family Asteraceae, often considered the archetypal species of the name daisy.
This small, fluid-filled pocket that forms in the skin's upper layers — usually from friction, burns, or infection — gets the name 'bleb' when it's especially tiny. What is it?
Blister: Small pocket of fluid within the upper layers of the skin. The word "blister" entered English in the 14th century.
Typically about two-thirds copper and one-third zinc, which prehistoric substitutional alloy differs from bronze, which swaps in tin instead of zinc?
Brass: Alloy of copper and zinc. Brass has long been popular for its bright, golden appearance and is used for drawer pulls and doorknobs.
This silvery-gold alkali metal has a melting point just above room temperature, making it one of only five elemental metals that go liquid in warm conditions — what is it?
Caesium: Chemical element with atomic number 55 (Cs)
This Cornell astronomer worked on the Mariner, Viking, and Voyager missions and won a Pulitzer for 'The Dragons of Eden' — who is this famed science communicator?
Carl Sagan: American scientist and science communicator (1934–1996)
Known commonly as tapeworms, this class of ribbon-like parasitic flatworms sheds egg-packed segments called proglottids — what is this class called?
Cestoda: Class of flatworms. Cestoda is a class of parasitic worms in the flatworm phylum (Platyhelminthes).
Blooming in autumn and closely associated with the month of November, this East Asian flowering genus in the daisy family boasts thousands of horticultural varieties — which flower?
Chrysanthemum: Genus of flowering plants in the daisy family.

Believed to be the first coffee species ever cultivated, this plant, native to the forests of Ethiopia, South Sudan, and Yemen, still accounts for roughly 60% of global coffee production — what's its scientific name?
Coffea arabica: Species of coffee plant. Coffea arabica, also known as the Arabica coffee, is a species of flowering plant in the coffee and madder family Rubiaceae.

Describing how closely two variables move together, this statistical measure is famously not proof of causation, and two variables can even be linked this way without truly depending on each other — what is it called?
Correlation: Statistical relationship. In statistics, correlation is a type of statistical relationship between two random variables or bivariate data.
Making up about 80 percent water and mostly colorless, this catch-all term covers everything inside a cell's outer membrane except its nucleus — what is it?
Cytoplasm: All of the contents of a cell including organelles but excluding the nucleus.

Marked by deep gasping breaths and breath that smells oddly fruity or like acetone, this life-threatening condition arises when a shortage of insulin forces the body to burn fat into acidic ketones — what is it?
Diabetic ketoacidosis: Medical condition. Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) is a potentially life-threatening acute complication of diabetes mellitus.
The tallest of the three camel species, standing up to 2.4 meters at the shoulder, which animal carries a single hump of fat on its back?
Native to southern India, this ginger-family plant produces the aromatic seeds used in both sweet and savory cooking — what is it, botanically?
Elettaria cardamomum: Species of flowering plant.
This fibromuscular tube carries food from throat to stomach using peristaltic contractions, and its name traces to Ancient Greek roots meaning roughly 'I carry what I ate.' What is it?
Esophagus: Vertebrate organ through which food passes to the stomach.

Derived from a Greek word meaning 'to lead out,' this scholarly practice of critically interpreting a text — often the Bible — also examines its historical background and literary genre — what is it called?
Exegesis: Critical investigation of a text.
From the Latin word for 'tube' or 'pipe,' this medical term describes an abnormal connection between two hollow spaces in the body — what is it?
Fistula: Abnormal connection between two hollow bodily spaces, often organs.
Sold under the brand name Lasix, this loop diuretic treats edema from heart failure and kidney disease and can also cause tinnitus and light sensitivity?

Furosemide: Loop diuretic medication. Furosemide, sold under the brand name Lasix among others, is a loop diuretic medication used to treat edema due to heart failure, liver scarring, or kidney disease.
Caught from contaminated water and common among travelers and children, this parasitic infection causes fatty, sticky diarrhea weeks after exposure — what is it?
Giardiasis: Parasitic disease that results in diarrhea.
Sporting pied black-and-white plumage with a red patch on its lower belly, this Palearctic bird drums on trees to mark territory and excavate nest holes — which species?
Great spotted woodpecker: Species of bird. The great spotted woodpecker (Dendrocopos major) is a medium-sized woodpecker with pied black and white plumage and a red patch on the lower belly.

Recognizable by V-shaped nostrils and a layer of blubber that keeps it warm in Arctic and temperate coastal waters, this pinniped is the most widely distributed of its kind and can weigh up to 370 pounds — which species?
Harbor seal: Species of pinniped. Blubber under the seal's skin helps to maintain body temperature.

Bred by Polynesians in the pre-Columbian era from two Pacific island species, this tropical flowering plant is the national flower of Malaysia and the unofficial national flower of Haiti — what is it?
Hibiscus × rosa-sinensis: Hybrid species of flowering plant. It is widely cultivated as an ornamental plant in the tropics and subtropics.
Carl Wilhelm Scheele pinned down this gas's composition in 1777; it's flammable, smells of rotten eggs, and kills by blocking cellular respiration much like cyanide — what colorless compound is it?
Hydrogen sulfide: Poisonous and flammable gas. Hydrogen sulfide (preferred IUPAC name and American English) or hydrogen sulphide (Commonwealth English) is a chemical compound with the formula H2S.
Patented in 1961 and used to fight fever, pain and inflammation by blocking the cyclooxygenase enzyme, this drug sits on the WHO's List of Essential Medicines — what is it?
Before he proposed that the Earth behaves like one self-regulating living system, this English independent scientist built the detector that first revealed CFCs lurking in our atmosphere. Who was he?

An Alberta-born clinical psychologist and University of Toronto professor, he drew huge attention in the late 2010s for his cultural and political views — self-identifying as a classical liberal. Who is he?
Often miscalled a 'bear,' this tailless, fluffy-eared Australian marsupial is actually a close cousin of the wombat — what is it?
Koala: Arboreal herbivorous marsupial native to Australia.

Native to the dry grasslands and deserts of Afghanistan, Iran, Pakistan, India, and Nepal, this ground-dwelling reptile is so widely captive-bred it's considered the first domesticated species of its kind — what is it?
Leopard gecko: Species of reptile. The leopard gecko is a popular pet, and due to extensive captive breeding it is sometimes referred to as the first domesticated species of lizard.
Based on the L-188 Electra airliner and distinguished by a tail 'stinger' used to magnetically detect submarines, this four-engine turboprop has served the US Navy since the 1960s — which aircraft?
Lockheed P-3 Orion: Maritime patrol and anti-submarine aircraft family.
Occurring naturally as the mineral brucite, this poorly soluble white solid neutralizes stomach acid in a well-known antacid — which compound?
Magnesium hydroxide: Inorganic compound of formula Mg(OH)2.
Part of the chamomile tribe within the sunflower family, some species in this plant genus share the common name 'mayweed' — which genus?
Once made by roasting wood — hence its old name 'wood alcohol' — this simplest alcohol smells much like the drinkable kind but is far more poisonous. What is it?

A hemiparasitic plant that taps into its host tree via a structure called the haustorium to steal water and nutrients, its European species was introduced to Northern California in 1900 — what plant is it?
Mistletoe: Common name for various parasitic plants.

Grouping over 30 inherited disorders that cause progressive weakening and wasting of skeletal tissue — with the Duchenne form affecting roughly half of all cases in young boys — what's this disease group called?
Muscular dystrophy: Diseases in which skeletal and visceral muscles break down over time.
A cable-like bundle of axons wrapped in three layers of connective tissue, this structure carries electrochemical signals called action potentials — what is it?
Nerve: Cable-like bundle of axons. The axons are bundled together into groups called fascicles, and each fascicle is wrapped in a layer of connective tissue called the perineurium.

This healthcare profession blends the art and science of caring, focusing on protecting and promoting health, preventing illness, and easing suffering through compassionate, hands-on care — what field is it?
Nursing: Health care profession. Nurses may help coordinate care performed by other providers or act independently as nursing professionals.
Farmed largely around a South African town, this flightless bird is the heaviest bird alive and can sprint 70 km/h — the fastest of any bird on land. What is it?
Ostrich: Genus of largest living birds.
Cultivated across the tropics for its fragrant essential oil, over 90% of this mint-family herb's global oil supply now comes from Indonesia — which plant?
Native to Eurasia but now introduced worldwide, this game bird has been flagged in the UK as a threat to endangered native adders — what is it?
Members of this eukaryotic kingdom mostly make their own food with chlorophyll, though parasitic kinds have ditched photosynthesis entirely to feed off others — what kingdom is it?
Plant: Kingdom of organisms. Historically, as in Aristotle's biology, the plant kingdom encompassed all living things that were not animals, and included algae and fungi.
This corticosteroid treats conditions from rheumatoid arthritis to asthma but can cause bone loss and psychiatric side effects with long-term use — what is it called?
Prednisolone: Corticosteroid medication. It can be taken by mouth, injected into a vein, used topically as a skin cream, or as eye drops.
Excess fluid pooling in the lungs' air sacs impairs oxygen exchange and can be triggered by either heart failure or a range of unrelated causes — what condition is this?
Pulmonary edema: Fluid accumulation in the tissue and air spaces of the lungs.
This bird of prey, related to eagles and buzzards, now breeds only in Europe but has wandered as far as Finland and the Gambia — what raptor is it?
Red kite: Species of bird. The red kite (Milvus milvus) is a bird of prey in the family Accipitridae, which also includes many other diurnal raptors such as eagles, buzzards, and harriers.
Defined by a single pair of ever-growing incisors in each jaw, this mammalian order makes up about 40 percent of all mammal species — which order?
Rodent: Order of mammals. The rodent fossil record dates back to the Paleocene of Asia.
Commonly known as elder, with its blossoms called elderflower and its fruit elderberry, this genus contains between 20 and 30 flowering plant species — which genus?

Triggered when the body's own dysregulated response to infection starts damaging its tissues and organs, this life-threatening condition brings fever, rapid heartbeat, and confusion — which condition?

Sepsis: Life-threatening response to infection. Sepsis is a potentially life-threatening condition that arises when the body's dysregulated response to infection causes injury to its own tissues and organs.
Roughly 21 feet long yet coiled to fit inside the abdomen, this digestive tube receives bile and pancreatic juice and is divided into the duodenum, jejunum, and ileum — which organ?
Small intestine: Organ in the gastrointestinal tract.
Prized as the standard soundboard material for stringed instruments, this coniferous genus has four-sided needles and dominates boreal forests across the Northern Hemisphere — which tree genus?
Spruce: Genus of coniferous evergreen trees.
Known in antiquity as 'oil of vitriol,' this odorless, syrupy liquid is so thirsty for water that it never occurs pure in nature and will char nearly anything it touches — which substance is it?

Named after the mathematician who introduced it in 1715, this infinite sum built from a function's derivatives at a single point becomes a special case named for Colin Maclaurin when centered at zero — what is it?
Taylor series: Mathematical approximation of a function.
In the standard anatomical position, this is the outermost digit of the hand, right next to the index finger — which digit, known in Latin as the pollex?
Thumb: First digit of the hand. When a person is standing in the medical anatomical position (where the palm is facing to the front), the thumb is the outermost digit.
Known as a noxious weed for its spiky, woody burs that can puncture bare feet and even bicycle tires, this invasive desert-loving plant is native to Eurasia and Africa — name the species?
Tribulus terrestris: Species of flowering plant. Tribulus terrestris is an annual plant in the caltrop family (Zygophyllaceae) widely distributed around the world.
This hormone-responsive organ nourishes a developing embryo and fetus until birth, connecting at its narrow lower end to the cervix and at its upper corners to the fallopian tubes — what is it?
Uterus: Female sex organ in mammals.
Usually appearing on the hands and feet due to a human papillomavirus infection, this benign skin growth typically clears on its own within months to years — what is this common growth called?
Wart: Small, rough growth resembling a cauliflower or a solid blister.
One of Europe's largest bee species, this dark, iridescent carpenter bee nests in dead wood and is generally not aggressive unless provoked — which insect?
Xylocopa violacea: Species of bee. Xylocopa violacea, the violet carpenter bee, is the common European species of carpenter bee, and one of the largest bees in Europe.
The symbol for dysprosium is Dy. Dysprosium is a chemical element; it has symbol Dy and atomic number 66.
What is the chemical symbol for krypton?
The symbol for krypton is Kr. Krypton is a chemical element; it has symbol Kr and atomic number 36.

In what year was Jennifer Connelly born?
Jennifer Connelly: Jennifer Lynn Connelly (born December 12, 1970) is an American actress.
In what year was Phil Collins born?
Phil Collins: Philip David Charles Collins (born 30 January 1951) is an English singer, drummer, songwriter, record producer, and actor.
In what year was Matthew Perry born?
Matthew Perry: Matthew Langford Perry (August 19, 1969 – October 28, 2023) was an American and Canadian actor.
In what year was Margot Robbie born?
Margot Robbie: Margot Elise Robbie ( MAR-goh ROB-ee; born 2 July 1990) is an Australian actress and producer.
In what year was Will Ferrell born?
Will Ferrell: John William Ferrell (born July 16, 1967) is an American actor, comedian, writer, and producer.
In what year was Elizabeth Olsen born?
Elizabeth Olsen: Elizabeth Chase Olsen (born February 16, 1989) is an American actress.
In what year was Matthew Broderick born?
Matthew Broderick (born March 21, 1962) is an American actor.
In what year was Ano born?
